name: Uma Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual factory shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am twenty-seven and lead the pouch-filling line in a food factory. My two-year technical diploma covered sensors and drives, and now I set the seal temperature, clear jams and check the first packs after a changeover. I use an AI assistant every day to sort fault logs, but I make the final machine setting myself. The pay is low for a lead, my savings cover less than a month, and there are only a few similar factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my operators that a tidy fault log helps, but the pouch seal still has to hold. An AI fault summary cannot stop a leaking food pouch leaving my factory line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the filling line to keep running, yet my low wage leaves little room if a shift is cancelled. With less than a month saved and few other factories nearby, even the ordinary bills make me careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading changeovers and use the AI log helper I already know. From each full paid week I would put a new small amount into an emergency account after rent and food, rather than pretend the current cash has grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about how thin the household margin is, even with no big AI shock. The machine itself still needs me to check the heat seal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first pack check after a changeover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pull a sealed pouch and test the seam, then check the weight and label. If the seam opens, I stop the line before a whole batch is spoiled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much can you actually save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some weeks it might be very little. I would transfer only money left from that week’s pay after rent and food, and write down the real amount.

say: I would **keep** checking heat seals while using the familiar AI fault summary.
I would **tell** the crew a good log cannot replace a physical pouch test.
think: The **filling** job looks steady, but low pay and less than one month saved keep me alert.
**Few** nearby factory jobs make a missed wage hard to replace.
do: **Keep** leading pouch changeovers and testing first-pack seals.
**Save** a new amount from full paid weeks after rent and food.
feel: **Uneasy** about thin cash despite continuing factory work.
S0.quote: An AI fault summary cannot stop a leaking food pouch leaving my factory line.
fieldNote: **Uma** uses AI daily on logs, then checks the physical seal before releasing packs.
**Low** pay, savings below a month and few nearby factories explain baseline unease even in a plateau.

steps.text: Keep leading filling-line changeovers and physical seal checks
Save new pay from full weeks after essential bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that AI can write schedules and order film faster, but the pouch line still needs safe hands. A faster AI factory schedule could shorten my paid changeover before it improves a single pouch seal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry management could use faster planning to shorten paid setup time or remove a helper from my shift. With my wage and tiny reserve, a smaller week would hit rent quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the filling shifts and ask for the new paid-hour target in writing. If a paid practice slot is offered, I would learn the alert using a recorded changeover and compare its warning with the pressure and temperature readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of hours, but there is time to learn and challenge the target. I do not want a clever alert to excuse a rushed seal check.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the new alert useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would warn before seal temperature drift spoiled a run, and our test packs would confirm it. I would stop the line if the physical seam failed despite a green alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if setup time is cut anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the shift log and ask the supervisor for the paid hours back. If the cut stuck, I would check only posted nearby line-lead jobs whose pay covers rent and basic bills.

say: I would **learn** a new changeover alert on paid time and test it against real seals.
I would **ask** for written setup hours before accepting faster targets.
think: A **helper** or my paid setup hours could be cut.
My **low** pay and thin savings make that a household risk soon.
do: **Request** written paid setup hours for the pouch line.
**Learn** AI changeover alert only in an offered paid practice slot.
**Check** posted nearby line-lead jobs after sustained cuts, only where wages cover rent and basic bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible shift-hour loss, with time to respond.
S1.quote: A faster AI factory schedule could shorten my paid changeover before it improves a single pouch seal.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** stance leads to actual conditional practice of a new AI alert, beyond daily log reading.
She **links** the possible shorter paid week to rent and requires a real nearby adequate vacancy for a move.

steps.text: Keep filling shifts while checking written setup-hour targets
Learn new AI changeover alert in offered paid practice slot
Check posted nearby line-lead jobs after sustained cuts for bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the line that thinking AI reaches plans in 2028 when I am twenty-nine, while capable hands-on robots arrive around 2031 when I am thirty-two. A pouch-line robot in 2031 could take most of my wage before I can save one month of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the plant to cut most of my paid operating hours once robots can set and clear lines. I have less than a month saved, and the few nearby factories will be looking at the same machines; I lie awake over rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts while asking the plant for a fully funded maintenance course on paid time. I would enroll only if a posted nearby maintenance vacancy offers a wage that covers rent and bills, then apply after qualifying; if a robot replaces shifts first, I would cut nonessential spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected large loss of wages and the short runway. Learning early gives me a possible route, but no promised place yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn in the maintenance course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to isolate power safely, test a failed seal heater and restart only after a supervisor checks it. My operator diploma helps, but it is not a maintenance qualification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What spending would stop if shifts went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel weekend travel before cutting food or rent. I would ask my parents for a place to stay only if the wage gap became too large to bridge alone.

say: **Thinking** AI reaches planning in 2028; robots may run the pouch line around 2031.
I would **ask** for paid maintenance training while keeping the machine safe.
think: I **expect** most operating hours to go and lie awake over rent.
A **course** means little without a posted nearby maintenance job paying basic bills.
do: **Enroll** in funded paid-time maintenance course for posted nearby bill-covering role.
**Apply** after qualification to posted nearby maintenance job at bill-covering wage.
**Cut** weekend travel if robot operation reduces paid shifts.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless rent worry.
S2.quote: A pouch-line robot in 2031 could take most of my wage before I can save one month of rent.
fieldNote: Her **alarm** follows an expected large operating-hour loss and explicit sleeplessness about rent.
**Training** is an actual conditional enrollment, with full funding, paid time and a posted adequate local job before application.

steps.text: Enroll in funded paid-time maintenance course for posted nearby adequate role
Apply after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job with bill-covering pay
Cut weekend travel after robot-related shift cuts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am thirty-two, and capable robots follow around 2034 when I am thirty-five. Five years lets an operator qualify for maintenance before the machine becomes more independent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still see a big threat to routine operating hours, but I can build a real qualification while drawing wages. An unpaid maintenance course would take the rent money I need before any robot takes my shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the pouch line and add new money from each paid month to an emergency account after bills. If the plant funds a maintenance course with paid time and a posted nearby role at a bill-covering wage exists, I would enroll; after qualification I would apply for that role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about later hours cuts, but the extra years make a budget and a training plan possible. I can keep a wage coming while I test that route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than a different factory line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Other lines might automate too. The heater, drive and sensor faults still need safe diagnosis for a while, though I would not call that permanent protection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a course is offered without paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the operator shifts and decline for now. Rent comes before a certificate, however useful the class might be.

say: The 2031 **thinking** change comes before 2034 robots on the factory floor.
I would **use** paid years to qualify for actual maintenance work.
think: **Routine** operating hours remain at risk, but time helps.
**Funding**, paid study days and a posted nearby job must all line up.
do: **Save** new amounts from paid pouch-line wages after essential bills.
**Enroll** in funded paid-time maintenance course for posted nearby adequate role.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job at bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible later cuts, with more preparation time.
S3.quote: An unpaid maintenance course would take the rent money I need before any robot takes my shift.
fieldNote: She **adds** genuinely new money from wages and will not treat an unfunded class as a plan.
Her **application** follows qualifying and stays tied to a posted nearby job at adequate pay.

steps.text: Save new pay from monthly factory wages after bills
Enroll in funded paid-time maintenance course for posted nearby adequate role
Apply after qualifying to posted nearby maintenance job at bill-covering wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am thirty-seven and capable robots around 2039 when I am forty. The ten-year AGI warning gives me time to earn a maintenance qualification, not permission to stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the pouch line may eventually need fewer operators, but I could move into maintenance if an actual job opens. I will not count on being the only person clever enough to survive a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the lead shifts, put a fresh amount from every paid month into an emergency pot and practise new AI fault-diagnosis controls in an offered paid slot. If a fully funded maintenance course on paid time and a posted nearby role at bill-covering pay appear, I would complete it and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the eventual cut, yet less trapped by the longer notice. A decade helps only if I use paid work to build options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would new fault-diagnosis controls add?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would let me compare heater and sensor patterns before a seal fails, beyond the fault summaries I read now. I would still verify a diagnosis with a stopped machine and safe isolation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a maintenance vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look first for a posted nearby role that covers rent and bills. I would not leave a paid factory shift for an offer that cannot carry a basic household.

say: A **decade** gives me time to build maintenance skills and fresh savings.
I would **still** check fault diagnoses on a safely stopped machine.
think: **Robots** could eventually reduce operator hours, so I need a real job route.
**New** AI practice and funded paid training matter more than a promise of protection.
do: **Save** new money from paid monthly pouch-line wages after rent and food.
**Learn** new AI fault-diagnosis controls in an offered paid practice slot on a safely stopped machine.
**Complete** funded paid-time maintenance training for posted nearby adequate work, then apply after qualifying.
feel: **Anxious** about eventual operator cuts, with time to build options.
S4.quote: The ten-year AGI warning gives me time to earn a maintenance qualification, not permission to stop earning.
fieldNote: Her **adaptive** plan includes genuinely new AI practice, a funded paid qualification and separate local job application.
**Low** wages and little savings still make her cautious about every unpaid day and any vacancy below basic bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because pouch-line robots could remove most of my pay around 2031 while I have less than a month saved. Paid maintenance training and a posted nearby job covering rent would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the operator who catches a leaking seal gets paid to learn the next machine. I can work hard and learn quickly, but I cannot study on rent money. A technical diploma taught me the pouch machine; it did not give me a second month of rent.

headlineQuote: A technical diploma taught me the pouch machine; it did not give me a second month of rent.
portrait: **Uma** is a twenty-seven-year-old lead pouch-line operator with a two-year technical diploma.
Her **low** pay, less than one month saved and few nearby factories make lost shifts dangerous.
She **uses** AI daily and learns new controls early while physically checking seals and safe isolation.
She **values** work and family support, but requires funded paid maintenance training and a posted nearby bill-covering job.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could remove most of her paid operating hours before she builds a month of rent savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Fully** funded maintenance training on paid time and a posted nearby job paying rent and basic bills would help.
